## What is a Revolution?

![][image1]  
*Panel 1 (left) explains what a revolution is and Panel 2 (right) explains Earth’s lopsided revolution.*

Let’s start with how the Earth goes around the Sun. As you may know, the Earth orbits, or “circles” around the Sun.

In terms of the Sun and the Earth, when the Earth orbits the Sun, it is called a **revolution** *(panel 1\)*. The way that the Earth revolves around the Sun is not a perfect circle—in fact, it is kind of oval-shaped and off-center, also known as an **elliptical orbit**. The part of the Earth’s revolution around the Sun that comes the closest to the Sun is called the **perihelion**—it is around 91,400,000 (91.4 million) miles from the center of the Earth to the center of the Sun. The part of Earth’s revolution around the Sun that is the farthest from the Sun is called the **aphelion**—it is approximately 94,500,000 (94.5 million) miles from the center of the Earth to the center of the Sun *(panel 2).*

## What is an Axis?

![][image2]  
*Panel 3 explains what an axis is.*

The Earth’s **axis** is an imaginary line/pole going through the center of the Earth from top to bottom, so it doesn’t actually exist. It’s the center of rotation for the earth, and is tilted at an angle of 23.5°. As such, the rotation of the earth actually occurs along this at 23.5° (panel 3).

## What Causes the Seasons?

![][image3]

*Panel 4 explains the misconception that people have about the reason for the seasons.*

Some people think that the seasons happen because Earth is physically closer to the Sun in the summer, while in the winter, Earth is physically farther away from the Sun. However, this is a misconception and is not accurate *(panel 4\)*. 

![][image4]  
*Panel 5 (left) explains what direct sunlight is, while Panel 6 (right) explains what indirect sunlight is.*

Before explaining how the seasons work, it is important to know what direct vs indirect sunlight is. Direct sunlight is essentially where the sun’s rays hit the Earth at a more direct angle, around 90° *(panel 5\)*, while indirect sunlight is where the sun’s rays hit the Earth at a less direct, shallower angle *(panel 6\)*.

When an area of the Earth has more direct sunlight, or an angle closer to 90°, the sun’s rays are dispersed, or spread out, on a smaller area. In contrast, when an area of the Earth receives less direct sunlight, this means that the sun’s rays are concentrated over a large area. This means that for indirect sunlight, there are fewer of the sun’s rays per square foot, compared to direct sunlight. When there are fewer of the sun's rays per square foot, the total energy per square foot is decreased, causing a colder temperature.

*![][image5]*

*Panel 7 (left) explains the actual reason we have for summer in the Northern Hemisphere, and Panel 8 (right) explains the actual reason we have for winter in the Northern Hemisphere.*

The seasons happen because of the Earth’s tilt of 23.5°\! The tilted axis always points in the same direction, so different parts of the Earth get more or less of the Sun’s direct rays. 

In the Northern Hemisphere summer, the North Pole tilts towards the Sun around June, which means that the Northern Hemisphere receives more of the Sun’s rays directly *(panel 7\)*. This means that the Southern Hemisphere is tilting away from the Sun and receives less direct sunlight, which makes it colder and is the reason why the Southern Hemisphere experiences winter in June. This doesn’t necessarily mean that the Earth itself is closer to the Sun, but because of the Earth’s tilt, the angle of the sunlight is more direct. 

In the Northern Hemisphere winter, the South Pole is tilting towards the Sun around December. This means that the Northern Hemisphere is at a position where it is recieves less direct sunlight *(panel 8\)*. In contrast, during this time, the Southern Hemisphere receives more direct sunlight (summer) because it tilts toward the sun..

## What Causes Day and Night?

![][image6]  
*Panel 9 shows what a rotation is and how it can cause day and night.*

The Earth not only goes around the Sun, but it also spins on its axis (the imaginary line) in a counterclockwise direction. Every full spin is called a **rotation** and lasts 24 hours (a day\!\!) *(panel 9\)*. 

Because Earth is, as you may know, a sphere, it is wider and bulges out towards the equator, and “thinner” towards the poles. Since the equator is 40,075 km (24,092 miles) long, it needs to cover all of that distance in 24 hours, so it rotates at a whopping speed of 1,600 km (1,000 miles) per hour\! Since the width of the poles, however, are much smaller than the equator, the poles move at a very slow 0.00008 kilometers (0.00005 miles) per hour.

When we are on the side of the Earth that faces the Sun, it is daytime. Since Earth spins, we are eventually on the side that faces away from the Sun, which is nighttime.

You may have noticed that during the summer, it remains brighter for longer and during the winter, it becomes darker earlier. This also happens because of the Earth’s tilt\! 

In the long summer days, the top half of Earth just so happens to lean towards the sun because of the tilt. The Earth still rotates, but when it’s day, the Northern Hemisphere tilts towards the sun. Because the Northern Hemisphere is tilted towards the sun, the sun travels very high across the sky and takes a long path across it, taking more time to disappear into the horizon. This is what causes the long, summer days.

The short winter days are just the opposite of the long summer days—the Northern Hemisphere leans away from the sun, so the sun’s path stays low and it takes a short path across it, which causes it to rise late and set early.

## Why Do We Have Leap Years?

![][image7]

*Panel 10 shows how long a revolution can be, without being rounded.*

Many people have heard that one revolution around the Sun is equal to a year, or 365 days. The truth is, that the number’s just a tiny bit off. The number 365 is rounded—the actual amount of days that it takes to orbit the sun is 365.24219 days, or 365 days, 5 hours, 48 minutes, and 56 seconds (*panel 10*). So technically, if you divide those numbers by 365, one day is technically 23 hours, 56 minutes, and 4 seconds, but we have also rounded it up to 24 hours. With every year that passes by, there would be extra hours that would be left unaccounted. As the years pile up, the seasons begin to shift and drift. Over a long period of time, the Northern Hemisphere’s summer season could happen during December\!

To solve this problem, we have added an extra day every four years, called a **leap year**. However, in reality, when adding the extra time up, the extra time would only amount to 23.262222 hours. This means that we make the calendar longer by over 44 minutes, which could *also* make the seasons drift.

To solve this new problem that arises from the solution to the previous, scientists made another rule. This means that not every four years is a leap year. The rule is that if a year is divisible by 100 and not divisible by 400, the leap year is skipped. For example, the years 1700, 1800, and 1900’s leap years were skipped. However, since the year 2000 is divisible by 100 and 400, the leap year wasn’t skipped. The year 2100 will actually be skipped since it’s divisible by 100 but not by 400\!

## Conclusion

So, what does this all mean? First of all, this means that the reasons for the seasons are mainly because of the Earth’s tilt. Key terms to remember is that a **revolution** is when the Earth orbits around the Sun, while a **rotation** is when the Earth makes a full spin on its **axis**, which is an imaginary line going through the center of Earth. Days and nights happen because the Earth rotates on its axis—the axis’ tilt is also the reason why we have shorter winter days and longer summer days\! Lastly, leap years happen because the revolution around the sun isn’t perfectly 365 days, so we have added an extra day every four years.
